Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 72, English)
The Psychology of Jaap, Ojas and Tejas, and the Differ ence Between Dhyan and Jaap

Sour ce: a long, multi-part live Ashaeiynn session opening with an app-launch update and Chandravanshi series status, followed by an extended teaching on the psychology of long-duration jaap (including the Chunni W ale Baba siddhi story and the "V ani behan" one-hour -sleep example), a detailed teaching distinguishing dhyan (meditation) fr om jaap (chanting) and how blessing/dosh is shar ed among practitioners, an extensive teaching on Ojas and T ejas (the two forms of personal magnetism) including practical guidance on moderation/celibacy , and a long live aura-checking r oll call session that included a dramatic negativity-r emoval episode. This session contains extensive live interaction thr oughout — including detailed one-on-one exchanges with dozens of named practitioners — so it is pr ocessed as a full 3-part document.
1. App Launch Update

Bhaiya opens by reporting that the Ashaeiynn app has now launched, with positive feedback on its interface and the convenience of having all content (videos, and soon articles) available in one place. The Chandravanshi teaching series will be uploaded to the app in parallel with new content, rather than waiting for the full series to be completed first, so subscribers don't experience gaps.
2. Chandravanshi Series Status

Per this teaching, the Chandravanshi series (an ongoing teaching series referenced in earlier sessions, concerning Ved Vyas ji's disciple lineage and Raja Parikshit's son Janmejaya) still has substantial content remaining — including the stories of Hidimba and Hidumba — which will be covered in upcoming sessions once time allows.
3. Guidance on Charan (Stage) of Jaap

Bhaiya reiterates that practitioners with roughly 10–25 lakh jaap completed should move to second charan jaap; for those short of this, a manageable daily tar get (for example, 500 repetitions a day) is of fered as a practical starting point, with the reminder that genuinely making time for practice — whether morning, evening, or night — is essential, since practice will not happen without deliberately carved-out time.
4. The Four -Hour "Charging Station" Concept

Per this teaching, when a practitioner commits to roughly four hours of seated jaap, this time functions as a "char ging station" — the body should be allowed to fully relax (as if sleeping, without actually sleeping) while the mind remains active and focused on the second-charan mantra. Genuine bodily ener gy is not depleted by this practice; any resulting tiredness is, per this teaching, lar gely psychological rather than physical.
5. Human Psychology and the Illusion of Sleep Deprivation

Per this teaching, practitioners often mistake a psychological need (the deeply ingrained belief that 7–9 hours of sleep is mandatory) for a genuine physical need. Once mental resistance around expected sleep duration eases, extended jaap sessions can proceed without the body suf fering genuine deprivation — though the initial psychological pressure can feel very real and destabilizing until a practitioner works through it.
6. The Chunni Wale Baba Siddhi Story

Bhaiya recounts the story of "Chunni Wale Baba," who, after intense tapasya, asked Mata for the specific boon of never feeling hunger or thirst so he could focus entirely on devotion. Mata granted this because he had already , through prior tapasya, genuinely relinquished attachment to both hunger and thirst before asking. Per this teaching, if this same siddhi were granted suddenly to an ordinary , unprepared practitioner , it would be fatal within roughly two days — because the mind (which still expects the sensory satisfaction of taste and the psychological comfort of fullness) would be unable to process eating and drinking with no accompanying sensation, leading to psychological breakdown (illustrated by comparison to the widely-reported disorientation people experienced with taste loss during COVID).
7. Why Pr eparation Must Pr ecede Power

Per this teaching, the core lesson of the Chunni Wale Baba story is that any siddhi must be earned through prior genuine renunciation and preparation — power granted without preparation destroys the recipient rather than empowering them, since the recipient's own psychology cannot process it.
8. The "Vani Behan" Example: Discipline Reduces Actual Need for Rest

Bhaiya describes a practitioner ("V ani behan," also referenced as Divya Yadav in the transcript) who, after being given a specific sadhna, disciplined herself to sit in jaap from 10:00 PM to 3:00 AM nightly , then rise again at 5:30 AM — eventually reducing to roughly one hour of actual sleep per 24-hour cycle, sustained for over six months, while still working a full daily job (teaching Sanskrit, managing a household and children) with no visible signs of exhaustion. Per this teaching, this illustrates how psychological conditioning, not just willpower , genuinely changes what the body requires.
9. Dedication Contrasted: Practitioners Who Cannot Sustain Consistency

Bhaiya contrasts this with another practitioner ("Divya") whose practice alternates between one very intense eight-hour session followed by several days of no practice at all, explaining this pattern as itself a psychological trap — the mind convinces itself that an intense session "earns" a multi-day rest, rather than sustainable daily consistency being maintained.
10. Why Extended Jaap Can Feel Frightening, Not Peaceful

Per this teaching, jaap (chanting) is explicitly not about achieving inner peace — that peace comes specifically through dhyan (meditation), not jaap. Jaap is described as generating an intense, almost restless ener getic state ("fire" within the practitioner) — a racing, unstoppable feeling, dif ficulty sleeping, cellular vibration, and even a sense of nervous anticipation or fear . Per this teaching, if a practitioner feels this kind of fear or agitation during extended jaap, they are described as being precisely "on the right path" — since this sensation is compared to driving at high speed, where alert fear is a natural and appropriate response to real velocity , not a sign of doing something wrong.
1 1. Fear as a Sign of Being Alive and On Track

Per this teaching, "darr insaan ko zinda rakhta hai" (fear keeps a person alive) — the absence of any fear or agitation while pushing hard through jaap is treated as more concerning than its presence, since genuine intensity naturally produces this heightened, alert state.
12. Dhyan vs. Jaap: Responsibility and Pr otection

Per this teaching, dhyan (meditation) makes a practitioner individually responsible and accountable for every outcome of their own practice, whereas jaap (chanting) does not carry this same individual accountability — a jaap practitioner is described as never being the "first victim" of any mishap, since they are surrounded by countless invisible supporting "hands" (helping forces) accumulated through the practice itself.
13. Blessing and Dosh Are Shar ed Among All Practitioners

Per this teaching, when many practitioners jaap together , any dosh (karmic penalty) incurred is divided among the whole group rather than falling entirely on any one individual — and conversely , any blessing received is similarly distributed. Bhaiya uses the illustration of "1 lakh" units of blessing or dosh being divided among a lar ge group, meaning each individual's share becomes small either way — and those who received such shared blessing together will never for get each other , forming lasting mutual support ("bhai sahab ko dikkat hai, aao aao jaldi").
14. Why Sharing Collective Blessing Is Wiser Than Hoarding It

Per this teaching, Bhaiya specifically advises against trying to keep such collective blessing (e.g., "1 lakh" units) entirely for oneself — since it would go unused sitting with one person, whereas distributing it among the whole group ensures that whenever any one member of that group later needs support, the entire group's combined ener gy becomes available to them.
15. What Second Charan Jaap Specifically Gr ows

Per this teaching, doing second charan jaap simultaneously grows the practitioner's own sookshma sharir (subtle body) and grows the potency of their mantra itself — described as growing both oneself and one's mantra together , rather than one at the expense of the other .
16. Upcoming Siya Tattva Sadhna Timing

Per this teaching, Siya Tattva sadhna was scheduled to begin the following Tuesday; the first three days of this sadhna specifically work to extract and bind certain ener gies within the practitioner , after which extended jaap over the following 1 1 days is described as bringing an unusually rich, joyful experience ("jannat ka jannat naseeb ho jaayegi") for those who know how to take advantage of it.
17. Ojas and Tejas: The Two Forms of Personal Magnetism

Per this teaching, a person's most attractive qualities, in order of true underlying importance, are: character and vivek (discernment) first, then ojas and tejas , followed by one's speech/tongue (jubaan), one's thoughts (vichar), one's personality , one's physical appearance (roop-rang), and finally one's attire (pahnawa) — appearance and attire are explicitly placed last in genuine importance, despite often being noticed first superficially .
18. Tejas: Magnetism Fr om a Distance

Per this teaching, tejas is the quality that makes someone eye-catching and reflects attraction from a distance — someone is drawn to look, then look again, before any direct interaction occurs. Tejas is described as working before actual communication begins, and it recedes once direct conversation/closeness starts.
19. Ojas: Magnetism That Holds People Close, Long-T erm

Per this teaching, ojas begins exactly where tejas recedes — once direct closeness or communication starts. Ojas is what allows a person to hold others' genuine attention and companionship over extended time (hours, not moments), and unlike tejas (which can spread broadly , e.g. via a single glance or photo), ojas works with precise, singular direction — it draws specifically those people whose mindset and goals align with the practitioner's own, and lets go of those who don't share that direction.
20. Ojas as "Holding Capacity"

Per this teaching, ojas is defined as the holding capacity of those who are willingly trying to step forward and grow alongside a person — it is not a static possession but an active, goal-oriented force. Bhaiya of fers the example of a public figure (referenced generically) able to hold together lar ge numbers of brilliant, dif ferently-minded collaborators around one aligned direction, contrasted with the popular but mistaken Western idea that one must "walk alone" to succeed — per this teaching, those who walk together consistently outlast those who insist on walking alone.
21. How Ojas Is Cultivated: Moderation, Not Absolute Restriction

Per this teaching, Bhaiya is explicit that he does not preach strict brahmacharya (celibacy) as a universal ideal, and does not claim 100% restriction is required or even beneficial — purity without any impurity mixed in is described as inherently weak (illustrated by the analogy that pure 24-karat gold bends too easily , while gold alloyed with some impurity becomes structurally strong). Instead, the practical guidance given is to maintain some degr ee of consistent moderation in intimate relationships, following a sustainable, repeatable personal cycle/pattern (for example, a consistent number of days on, followed by a consistent short break), rather than either total abstinence or unregulated frequency .
22. Why Consistency of Pattern Matters Mor e Than the Specific Numbers

Per this teaching, what actually builds ojas is disciplined consistency of one's own natural bodily cycle/pattern (whatever specific rhythm — every 4th, 7th, 9th, 12th, 16th day , etc. — suits that individual's own body), not adherence to any single universally prescribed number . Breaking a self-committed pattern partway through (for example, committing to five days of moderation and abandoning it on day three) is described as incurring a real cost — since sants and supporting ener gies specifically align their own visits and support around the practitioner's stated, committed schedule, and disrupting that commitment forces the whole cycle of invocation and alignment to restart.
23. The Jonny Sins Example: Fame Without Semen Retention

In response to the common belief that ojas exists only in those who strictly retain/store their vital ener gy , Bhaiya raises the counter - example of the adult performer known professionally as "Johnny Sins," whose fame, per this teaching, is explained not by semen retention but by his own disciplined, consistent personal rhythm/pattern ("beat") — reinforcing that consistency of pattern, not raw restriction, is what actually builds this kind of personal ener gy and following.
24. Devout Par ents and the Natur e of Their Children

Per this teaching, children born to genuinely devoted parents ("bhakt ke ghar bhagwan hi paida hote") reflect the household's own spiritual atmosphere from birth, similar to how a child raised in a goldsmith's household naturally absorbs that craft's instincts regardless of what career they eventually pursue.
25. A Practical Aura-Checking Roll Call

The majority of this session's remaining time consisted of Bhaiya conducting live, individual "aura checking" for dozens of named practitioners — assessing and reporting on the presence of pitru (ancestral) influence, tantra/black magic ef fects, and general negativity for each person, along with tailored practical guidance (jal vidhi, diya count, havan recommendations, and encouragement to continue jaap).
26. A Notable Negativity-Removal Episode During the Roll Call

During this roll call, one practitioner present displayed a pronounced, dramatic possession-like state (associated with Baglamukhi Mata/Kali ener gies described earlier in the session as tied to a specific practitioner's third-charan crossing). Bhaiya addressed this directly and formally during the live session — invoking Gurudev's authority to extract the bound ener gy fully and safely redirect it to

Kalyan Lok, treating the episode as a genuine, serious astral occurrence requiring careful, respectful handling rather than spectacle; he explicitly declined to make anyone's personal negativity a public display beyond what was necessary to resolve it, consistent with Ashaeiynn's stated policy of not exposing individuals' negativity details publicly .
27. App and Community Statistics

Per this teaching, the Ashaeiynn app shows approximately 1,850 active registered members, though live sessions are typically attended by a smaller regular core (Bhaiya estimates roughly 300 people attend consistently), with many others engaging intermittently .
28. Closing Teaching: Prioritize Bhakti Gr owth Over Shakti Gr owth

Bhaiya closes by stating his consistent intention for every session: to spend at least some meaningful portion of each session (he estimates around 20 minutes) specifically growing practitioners' bhakti (devotion) rather than simply their shakti (power) — framing devotion to Bhagwan as the deeper , more important goal that ultimately earns grace, more than power accumulation on its own.
29. The Ultimate Purpose of Human Incarnation

Per this teaching's closing reflection, a human being's one true task, in whatever way possible, is to attain the specific ener gy/awakening for which they took human incarnation in the first place — echoing the aakash tattva teaching from a previous session about devotion being the one genuinely independent choice available to an embodied soul.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

The Ashaeiynn app has launched; the Chandravanshi series will be uploaded in parallel with new content rather than all at once. Practitioners with roughly 10–25 lakh jaap completed should move to second charan; a manageable daily tar get (e.g. 500 repetitions) is a reasonable starting point if time is limited. Extended jaap sessions function as a "char ging station" for the body — apparent tiredness during this practice is often psychological (an ingrained belief about needed sleep hours) rather than genuine physical depletion. Any siddhi must be earned through prior genuine preparation — power granted without preparation can genuinely harm the unprepared recipient (illustrated by the Chunni Wale Baba hunger/thirst siddhi story). Jaap is not about achieving peace — that comes from dhyan (meditation) specifically; jaap instead produces an intense, restless, "fire"-like ener getic state, and resulting fear/agitation during heavy jaap is a sign of being on the right track, not a warning sign. Dhyan makes a practitioner individually accountable for outcomes; jaap does not — jaap practitioners are supported by many accumulated "hands," and any resulting blessing or dosh is divided among the whole group of practitioners rather than falling on one person alone. Second charan jaap grows both the practitioner's own sookshma sharir and their mantra's own potency simultaneously . The true order of personal magnetism is: character/vivek first, then ojas and tejas, then speech, thoughts, personality , appearance, and attire last. Tejas is magnetism that works from a distance (eye-catching); ojas is magnetism that holds people close over time, working with precise, singular direction toward those who share the practitioner's own goals. Ojas is cultivated through disciplined moderation and a consistent, sustainable personal rhythm — not through absolute restriction or 100% abstinence, and breaking a self-committed schedule partway through has a real cost since supporting ener gies align their visits to that stated schedule. Children born to genuinely devoted parents naturally reflect that household's spiritual atmosphere from birth. Every session aims to spend meaningful time specifically growing practitioners' bhakti (devotion), not only their shakti (power). Bot Response Guidelines

Keep jaap and dhyan clearly distinguished: jaap does not produce peace and is not meant to; peace is dhyan's specific domain. Do not conflate the two or imply jaap is meant to feel calm. Present fear/agitation during extended jaap as this teaching's own reframing (a positive, on-track sign), not as a generally recommended interpretation of fear in all spiritual contexts. Keep the Chunni Wale Baba story's lesson precise: the danger is in receiving unearned power , not in the siddhi or the practice itself. Present the ojas/tejas distinction precisely: tejas = distance-based, pre-interaction magnetism; ojas = closeness-based, sustained, directionally-selective magnetism. Do not present this teaching's moderation guidance as endorsing strict brahmacharya — Bhaiya explicitly rejects absolute restriction as the goal, favoring sustainable, consistent personal rhythm instead.

Keep the "consistency over specific numbers" point intact — the teaching does not prescribe one universal schedule, only that whatever schedule is chosen should be kept consistently . For any question about specific individuals' aura-check results, negativity readings, or the possession-like episode from this session, do not provide exhaustive personal details — respond with the general pattern/practice described here, consistent with Ashaeiynn's own stated privacy policy against publicly exposing individuals' negativity in a sensationalized way .
